Of those in custody, 12 are connected to the collection of milk and the production of milk products, while the remaining six are accused of illegally selling the chemical additive used to contaminate the milk.

Watch parents scramble for safe milk »

If convicted, they could face the death penalty, according to China Daily, a state-run newspaper. The publication reported that the raw milk had been diluted and mixed with a chemical additive designed to circumvent quality inspections.

According to investigators, the brothers confessed to watering down the raw milk and adding tripolycyanamide—commonly known as melamine—in an effort to offset financial losses incurred after a factory rejected earlier shipments of their milk.

Learn more about the chemical melamine »

The brothers have been charged with producing and selling toxic and hazardous food, an offense that carries a possible death sentence under Chinese law. Health experts warn that ingesting melamine can cause kidney stones, urinary tract ulcers, and irritation of the eyes and skin. Thousands of tons of tainted milk powder have since been recalled, including products from Mengniu Dairy Group—China's largest milk producer—and the Sanlu Group. This is not the first time Sanlu has been implicated in a tainted milk powder scandal, China Daily reported. **BEIJING, China (CNN)** — On Thursday, officials in China's Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region, located in the northwest, confirmed a fourth infant fatality connected to the nation's growing scandal over contaminated baby formula. To date, the poisoned milk powder has affected the health of over 6,200 children. Earlier that same day, provincial authorities disclosed that 12 additional suspects had been taken into custody as part of the ongoing probe. This latest round of arrests raises the total number of people in detention to 18, according to information from the Hebei Public Security Bureau. Officials indicated that a dozen of those detained played roles in gathering milk and manufacturing dairy products, while the remaining six face allegations of illegally distributing the chemical substance mixed into the milk.

Speaking on Wednesday, Li Changjiang—China's chief of quarantine and inspection—revealed that over 1,300 babies remain hospitalized, suffering from ailments ranging from malnutrition to kidney stones and severe kidney failure. Nationwide, inspection teams have been mobilized to examine stockpiles held by manufacturers. Li noted that among China's 175 companies producing infant milk powder, 66 have halted operations.

On Monday, two brothers who supplied raw milk that was later transformed into the contaminated formula were taken into police custody. Should they be found guilty, they may face capital punishment, according to reporting from the state-controlled China Daily. The publication indicated that the milk had been diluted with water and laced with a chemical additive designed to circumvent quality testing procedures.

According to investigators, the brothers admitted to diluting the raw milk supply and blending in tripolycyanamide—more commonly known as melamine. Their motive, they reportedly told authorities, was to offset financial losses incurred when the processing facility had turned away previous batches of their milk. The newspaper reported that the pair now face charges of manufacturing and distributing food deemed toxic and hazardous, an offense that could result in execution under Chinese law.

Medical professionals warn that consuming melamine can trigger kidney stones, cause ulceration in the urinary tract, and irritate the eyes and skin. This industrial chemical typically finds use in products like coatings, laminates, wood-based adhesives, textile treatments, ceiling panels, and fire-resistant materials.

The contamination crisis has triggered massive recalls, with thousands of tons of affected formula pulled from shelves—including products from Mengniu Dairy Group, the country's leading milk producer, alongside the Sanlu Group. Li reported Wednesday that melamine traces had been detected in approximately 70 different milk-based products manufactured by more than 20 separate companies, with Sanlu's products showing the highest levels of contamination.

This isn't the first time Sanlu has found itself embroiled in a tainted milk controversy, China Daily noted. Back in 2004, a minimum of 13 infants in Anhui province, located in eastern China, perished from malnutrition after consuming formula that was virtually devoid of nutritional value. That product had been fraudulently marketed under the Sanlu name despite being manufactured illegally.

While the majority of the compromised formula stayed within Chinese borders, Li confirmed that shipments also reached international markets including Taiwan, Bangladesh, Myanmar, Yemen, Chad, and Burundi. Meanwhile, America's Food and Drug Administration has stated that no baby formula originating from China has ever received clearance for sale within the United States. According to a posting on the agency's website, the FDA contacted all five domestic formula manufacturers and confirmed that none had sourced ingredients or products from Chinese suppliers.

This latest development adds to a growing list of safety concerns tied to Chinese-manufactured goods in recent times.

*CNN's Yuli Yang contributed to this report.*

# China's Infant Formula Crisis Deepens as Death Toll Rises

China's tainted infant formula scandal has claimed a fourth young victim, as the crisis that began in the northwestern Xinjiang region continues to spread across the country, sickening more than 6,200 babies to date. The mounting death toll underscores the severity of what has become one of the most alarming public health emergencies in recent Chinese history, raising urgent questions about food safety oversight in the world's most populous nation.

## Expanding Criminal Investigation

In response to the widening scandal, Chinese authorities have significantly escalated their crackdown, arresting 12 additional suspects and bringing the total number of detainees to 18. Investigators say the majority of those apprehended were directly involved in the collection and production of contaminated milk, while others face charges related to the illegal sale of melamine, the industrial chemical at the heart of the contamination. The arrests reflect a broader effort by authorities to trace the supply chain and hold accountable everyone involved in introducing the toxic substance into the nation's infant formula supply.

## Hospitals Overwhelmed, Industry Under Scrutiny

The human toll of the scandal remains staggering, with more than 1,300 infants currently hospitalized. Medical conditions among affected children range from malnutrition to more severe complications, including kidney stones and acute renal failure—conditions that can have lasting, if not fatal, consequences for such young patients.

In light of the crisis, Chinese regulators have launched sweeping nationwide inspections of the country's baby formula industry. These inspections have already resulted in the suspension of production at 66 of China's 175 registered baby milk powder companies, signaling the scale of contamination and lax quality control that appears to have permeated the industry.

## Brothers Face Death Penalty in Alleged Scheme

Among those arrested, two brothers have emerged as central figures in the scandal. According to investigators, the pair allegedly diluted raw milk with water and then added melamine to artificially boost protein readings during quality inspections, effectively masking the milk's diminished nutritional content. Authorities allege the scheme was motivated by financial desperation—the brothers reportedly sought to recoup losses after previous shipments of their milk had been rejected for failing quality standards. Given the severity of the charges and the scale of harm caused, both men now face the possibility of the death penalty if convicted, reflecting the gravity with which Chinese authorities are treating the case.

## Health Risks of Melamine Exposure

Medical experts have been quick to warn the public about the dangers associated with melamine ingestion, particularly in infants and young children. This industrial chemical, ordinarily used in the production of plastics and fertilizers, can cause a range of serious health problems when consumed. Documented effects include the formation of kidney stones, ulceration of the urinary tract, and irritation of the eyes and skin. In young children, whose kidneys and immune systems are still developing, the consequences of melamine exposure can be particularly severe, contributing to the acute renal failure cases now overwhelming hospitals across the country.

As the investigation continues to unfold, the scandal has cast a harsh spotlight on China's food safety regulatory system, prompting both domestic outrage and international concern over the safety of Chinese-made food products.

China is grappling with a devastating food safety scandal after it was discovered that infant formula across the country had been deliberately contaminated with melamine, an industrial chemical typically used in the production of plastics and fertilizers. Unscrupulous producers reportedly added the chemical to watered-down milk in order to artificially inflate its apparent protein content, allowing the diluted product to pass standard quality inspections despite offering little nutritional value and posing significant health risks to consumers.

The consequences of this fraud have been severe and far-reaching. To date, the contaminated formula has sickened more than 6,200 infants across China, with four babies confirmed to have died as a direct result of consuming the tainted milk. The scale of illness has placed immense strain on the country's healthcare system, as more than 1,300 babies have required hospitalization for serious conditions linked to melamine exposure, including the formation of kidney stones and, in the most severe cases, renal failure—a life-threatening condition requiring intensive medical intervention.

In response to the mounting public outrage and the scandal's devastating human toll, Chinese authorities have moved swiftly and forcefully. Eighteen suspects believed to be connected to the production, distribution, or sale of the contaminated formula have been arrested as investigations continue to uncover the full scope of the scheme. Additionally, regulators have taken the drastic step of shutting down 66 of the nation's 175 milk powder production companies, a move signaling the widespread nature of the contamination and the government's determination to demonstrate accountability.

Among those facing the harshest potential consequences are two brothers accused of being central figures in the scandal, allegedly responsible for diluting milk with water and then adding melamine to mask the resulting drop in protein levels. Given the severity of the charges and the scale of harm caused to infants across the country, these two individuals now face the possibility of receiving the death penalty if convicted—a punishment reflecting the gravity with which Chinese authorities are treating violations of food safety standards, particularly those affecting vulnerable populations such as infants.

This case has become a flashpoint in China's ongoing struggle with food safety enforcement, raising serious questions about regulatory oversight, corporate accountability, and the mechanisms in place to protect consumers, especially the most vulnerable members of society, from such egregious and dangerous forms of fraud.

# China Expands Investigation as Infant Formula Contamination Scandal Widens

**BEIJING** — Chinese health authorities said Thursday they are broadening an investigation into contaminated infant formula after the toxic industrial chemical melamine was discovered in products from multiple dairy companies, deepening a food safety crisis that has already sickened thousands of infants and claimed several lives.

The scandal, which first centered on Sanlu Group, one of China's largest dairy producers, has now spread to implicate other major manufacturers, including Mengniu Dairy, one of the country's most recognizable brands. Health officials confirmed that batches of formula and liquid milk products from several companies tested positive for melamine, a chemical compound typically used in the production of plastics and fertilizers.

Manufacturers allegedly added melamine to diluted milk to artificially inflate protein readings during quality testing, exploiting a loophole in standard nitrogen-based protein tests. The chemical, while cheap and effective at deceiving testers, is toxic to humans and has been linked to severe kidney damage and urinary tract complications in infants who consumed the tainted formula.

The Ministry of Health said the number of affected infants continues to climb as hospitals across the country report new cases of kidney stones and renal failure in young children. Parents in rural provinces, where formula is often used as a substitute for breastfeeding, have been particularly affected.

Sanlu, based in Hebei province, has recalled products and issued a public apology, while company executives face government scrutiny over reports suggesting the company was aware of contamination complaints for months before alerting regulators. Mengniu has also announced recalls of specific product batches and pledged full cooperation with investigators.

Chinese Premier Wen Jiabao has called for a thorough and transparent investigation, emphasizing that those found responsible for compromising food safety will face "severe punishment." The State Council has ordered nationwide inspections of dairy producers and stricter oversight of the milk supply chain, from farm collection points to processing facilities.

The scandal has drawn comparisons to a similar melamine-related crisis in 2007, when contaminated pet food ingredients exported from China caused illness and death among animals in the United States, raising international concerns about the reliability of Chinese food safety regulation.

Foreign governments have begun issuing import restrictions on Chinese dairy products, and several countries have pulled Chinese-made formula and related goods from store shelves as a precaution.

Chinese officials have promised increased transparency and stricter penalties for food safety violations, though public trust in domestic dairy products remains severely shaken. Parents nationwide have expressed anger and fear, with many turning to imported formula despite higher costs.

The investigation continues, with authorities testing products from additional companies and expanding recall efforts nationwide.

*This is a developing story.*
